lesson.title: A Real Example: The Peppered Moth
lesson.subject: science

contentBlocks.text: You've learned the four requirements of natural selection. Today: a real, well-documented example!

The peppered moth is a classic, well-documented example of natural selection observed within a human lifetime. Before industrial pollution darkened tree bark in parts of England, light-colored peppered moths were well camouflaged against light, lichen-covered trees, while darker moths stood out to predators. As pollution darkened the tree bark, the camouflage advantage flipped: darker moths became better camouflaged and light moths became easier for birds to spot, so the population's proportion of dark-colored moths increased significantly over just a few decades. Walk through this example using all four requirements of natural selection from yesterday's lesson: identify the variation, the inheritance, the overproduction, and the differential survival.
You just applied all four requirements of natural selection to a real example! Tomorrow we'll look at the evidence for evolution more broadly.

objectives: Understand the peppered moth as a real, documented example of natural selection
Identify all four requirements of natural selection within this example
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's four requirements of natural selection briefly.
2. Introduce the peppered moth example and its pollution/camouflage connection.
3. Have the child identify all four requirements within the example.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's broader-evidence lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: walk through just one requirement at a time (start with variation — light vs. dark moths already existed) before asking for all four together
Ready for more: ask the child to predict what would happen to the moth population if pollution controls later cleaned the tree bark back to its original light color
This is a real, well-documented case study, not a hypothetical — worth emphasizing that natural selection can be observed happening within a human lifetime, not only over geologic time
teacherGuide.answerKey: Variation: both light and dark moths already existed in the population. Inheritance: moth coloring is passed from parents to offspring. Overproduction: more moths were born than could survive predator attacks. Differential survival: as pollution darkened tree bark, dark moths were better camouflaged and survived/reproduced more successfully than light moths, shifting the population's proportions over time.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS Grade 9-10 standard HS-LS4-2, applying natural selection's mechanism to a real, well-documented historical example.
